strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored question: how the component configuration (r1, r2, r) of Kronecker adapters determines both theoretical properties and empirical performance. The framing of component design as a first-class design axis, with LoRA and KronA as special cases (Table 1), is clean and clarifying.

The theoretical analysis is reasonably rigorous and self-contained: the subspace alignment result (Theorems 3.2/B.1 and C.1) built on the Kronecker-product SVD, with full proofs provided in the appendix, plausibly explains the observed asymmetry between r1 and r2 (e.g., the exp(−d_in r1/r2) term favors small r1 and large r2, consistent with Tables 2-4).

The training stabilization strategy (Theorem 3.4, scaling λ = α/√(r·r2)) is a practical and well-motivated contribution, supported by gradient-norm evidence in Figure 1 and an ablation over initialization strategies (Table 8).

Experiments are reasonably broad: GLUE on T5-Base, mathematical reasoning and code generation on LLaMA-2-7B, plus LLaMA-3.1-8B for scalability, with three random seeds and standard deviations. The computational cost analysis (Table 12) and the equivalent reformulation in Eq. (17) show CDKA matches LoRA in time and memory, addressing the main practical objection to Kronecker adapters.

The empirical headline results are meaningful: 87.30 GLUE average with only 0.41M parameters (0.18% of full fine-tuning), SOTA on GSM8k for both LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, and a substantial improvement over KronA under the same budget.
weaknesses: The closest related work, MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025), which already performs heterogeneous component design for Kronecker adapters, is excluded from all experiments with only a brief justification ('substantial computational overhead'). Given that CDKA's core contribution is principled component design for exactly this method class, the absence of a direct comparison to MoKA (and MoKA-MoE) weakens the significance claims considerably; the 'state-of-the-art' claims are only established against LoRA variants.

The link between the theoretical quantities and the derived principles is loose. Remark 3.3's principles follow from heuristically interpreting bounds on the initialization scale α and convergence time t*, but no formal argument connects alignment with the first-step gradient of full fine-tuning to downstream task performance. The analysis also inherits strong restrictions from LoRA-One (linear model, isotropic sub-Gaussian inputs, single-layer), which are not revisited.

There are internal inconsistencies between the stated principles and the empirical evidence. Principle 1 claims increasing r1 degrades performance, yet Table 3 is non-monotonic (49.93 at r1=2 vs. 49.89 at r1=16), and Table 6 shows performance is essentially flat when r1 and r2 increase jointly. More strikingly, the deployed GLUE configuration (r1=3, r2=3, r=1) contradicts the paper's own guidance (small r1, large r2, r ≥ r*), suggesting the guidelines are not consistently applied even by the authors.

Much of the theoretical machinery is directly adapted from Zhang et al. (2025) (Lemmas B.2, B.4, C.2, E.4 are explicitly adapted from LoRA-One and Stöger & Soltanolkotabi), so the novelty of the theory is incremental; the core contribution is transferring an existing analysis framework to the Kronecker parameterization.

Theorem 3.4's 'if and only if' claim is supported by an informal scaling argument (Eqs. 44-46) with O(λ²) remainders rather than a fully rigorous proof, and Figure 1b shows the gradient norms still fluctuate noticeably after stabilization, so the practical benefit is modest.

Evaluation is confined to NLP tasks and relatively small-scale fine-tuning (7B/8B models, single epoch); there is no evidence on other modalities (despite Kronecker adapters' popularity in diffusion models) or on larger models, limiting the reach of the conclusions.

No mention of code release, and several key results are sourced from third-party papers (He et al., 2025) with only partial reimplementation, which complicates reproducibility of the comparison tables.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored question: how the component configuration (r1, r2, r) of Kronecker adapters affects performance, going beyond the common 'more attainable rank is better' heuristic. Table 2 (same attainable rank, different configurations, up to ~2.6 point differences) is a convincing motivating observation.

The theoretical framework is coherent: the analysis via Kronecker-product SVD (Definition 2.1) and the subspace-alignment result (Theorem B.1, simplified as Theorem 3.2) adapts the now-standard LoRA-One analysis machinery to the Kronecker setting, and the derived principles are mostly consistent with the empirical trends in Tables 3-7.

The training-stability analysis (Theorem 3.4, scaling factor λ = α/√(r·r2)) addresses a real practical failure mode (gradient collapse under some configurations, Figure 1a), and the empirical computational-cost comparison (Table 12) shows CDKA matches LoRA in time and memory.

Experiments cover multiple task families (GLUE subset, mathematical reasoning, code generation) and two backbone scales (LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), with three seeds and variance reported, and the final method uses far fewer trainable parameters than LoRA-based baselines (0.41M vs 3.24M on T5-Base).
weaknesses: The two most closely related baselines, MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025) and MoKA-MoE (Yu et al., 2025), are excluded from all main comparisons on the grounds of 'substantial computational overhead'. Since the paper's central claim is that principled component design makes Kronecker adapters competitive, the absence of these direct competitors substantially weakens the empirical case; no quantified overhead comparison or at least an ablation against MoKA's configuration is provided.

Several headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. On GLUE (Table 9), CDKA (87.30) is below LoRA-One (88.73), GoRA (87.96), and LoRA-GA (87.77), yet the abstract describes 'near-optimal performance on NLU'; on HumanEval, CDKA (24.59±2.74) is statistically indistinguishable from GoRA (24.80±1.04) despite being labeled 'second best'.

The validation of the three principles in Remark 3.3 relies on a single task (GSM8k, LLaMA-2-7B) with a 100K subset. Principle 1 ('increasing r1 degrades performance') is weakly supported: in Table 3, r1=16 (49.89±0.27) matches r1=2 (49.93±1.25), and Table 6 shows performance is essentially flat as r1 grows from 2 to 16 under a fixed budget, contradicting a monotone-degradation reading.

The theory rests on strong simplifying assumptions (linear model, isotropic sub-Gaussian inputs, Gaussian gradient structure) whose disconnect from transformer fine-tuning is never bridged; moreover, the design guidelines hinge on r* — the rank of the first-step full-fine-tuning gradient — which is unknown in practice, and the paper's own guidance ('r* ∈ [2, 8]') is a heuristic rather than a principled procedure, somewhat undercutting the 'principled design' framing.

There are internal inconsistencies in the method description: Theorem 3.2 assumes Gaussian initialization of A while Theorem 3.4 and the final method use Kaiming initialization; Table 8 shows the choice of init changes results by up to ~5 points, and the interaction between initialization, the scaling factor λ, and component configuration is not analyzed.

Some technical statements are imprecise: Theorem 3.4 claims the gradient norm is 'irrelevant to r1, r2 and r if and only if' λ ∈ Θ(1/√(r·r2)), but the proof only establishes leading-order scaling Θ(λ²rr2) under first-order approximations (Eqs. 42-43) and does not verify the 'only if' direction or control the O(λ²) remainder.

The variance bounds in Theorem B.1 involve constants and quantities (ξ, κ, σr*(G0)) that are not estimated for realistic settings, so it is unclear whether the assumed initialization scale α in Eq. (12) is attainable in practice; the theory-to-practice link is asserted rather than demonstrated.

No code release is mentioned, and reproduction requires the authors' specific hyperparameter choices (per-task configurations in Table 13 and Section 4.2 are tuned per dataset), which limits reproducibility and raises concerns that the reported gains depend on per-task tuning that baselines did not receive equally.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies component design (r1, r2, r) as an underexplored but important factor in Kronecker adapters, and formalizes it within a general formulation (Eq. 2) that unifies LoRA and KronA as special cases (Table 1).

The theoretical analysis grounded in the Kronecker product SVD extends the subspace-alignment framework of LoRA-One (Zhang et al., 2025) to Kronecker adapters. Theorem 3.2/B.1 provides concrete, checkable predictions (alignment probability and convergence time depend on r1, r2, r), and the proof structure (linear dynamics + error bound + Wedin-type argument) is coherent.

The derived principles (small r1, large r2, moderate r) are validated with a systematic ablation (Tables 2–8) that isolates each hyperparameter and also considers fixed-parameter-budget comparisons (Tables 6–7), showing genuine engagement with the practical constraints.

The scaling factor λ = α/√(r·r2) with a stability condition (Theorem 3.4) addresses a real practical problem (gradient collapse under different configurations, Figure 1), and the initialization ablation (Table 8) justifies the A/Kaiming, B/zero design.

Strong headline results on the NLG side: SOTA on GSM8k with LLaMA-2-7B (56.71 vs. LoRA-One 55.40) and parity with full fine-tuning on LLaMA-3.1-8B (73.74 vs. 73.69), at a parameter budget far below LoRA baselines, with training time and memory essentially identical to LoRA (Table 12).
Results are reported as mean ± std over three random seeds, and experimental details (hyperparameters in Appendix A, efficient reformulation in Eq. 17) support reproducibility reasonably well.
weaknesses: The closest competing methods are excluded from all empirical comparisons. MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025) and MoKA-MoE (Yu et al., 2025) are described in Section 2.2 as the most directly related work, yet the paper only compares against KronA. Excluding them 'since they introduce substantial computational overhead' weakens the SOTA claims on GSM8k and HumanEval; at minimum, MoKA (which shares CDKA's formulation and does not necessarily carry MoE overhead) should be benchmarked under matched budgets.

The NLU claims are overstated. On GLUE (Table 9), CDKA (87.30) ranks behind LoRA-One (88.73), GoRA (87.96), full fine-tuning (87.91), and LoRA-GA (87.77); 'near-optimal performance' and 'approach the performance of full fine-tuning' are generous characterizations of a 4th-place result, even accounting for the smaller parameter budget.

Some empirical evidence for the principles is thin or inconsistent with the theory. In Table 3, r1=2 (49.93) vs. r1=16 (49.89) shows essentially no degradation, and the text itself concedes only 'slight improvements' for small r1. The r* boundary in the guidelines is admitted to be an empirical guess (r* ∈ [2,8]), so the bridge from theory to the practical recipe is looser than the presentation suggests.

The deployed configurations in the main experiments (r1=r2=3, r=1 on GLUE) sit in tension with the paper's own guidelines (small r1, large r2, r ≥ r* with r* ∈ [2,8]), suggesting the final recipe relies on per-task tuning rather than the derived principles.

The theory relies on strong simplifications: a linear loss, isotropic sub-Gaussian inputs, first-step gradient alignment only, and Gaussian initialization. Theorem 3.4's 'if and only if' claim about gradient-norm invariance is derived via heuristic order-of-magnitude arguments (O(λ²) truncations) rather than a rigorous bound, and the abstract conditions (e.g., knowing r* = rank of the reshaped gradient) are not verifiable in practice.

Validation of the principles uses only one task (GSM8k) and one model (LLaMA-2-7B); several margins (e.g., Table 5: 54.56 vs. 54.18 vs. 54.26) are within or near one standard deviation, making the 'principles' partially noise-sensitive. Evaluation is limited to NLP, with no vision or multimodal tasks despite Kronecker adapters' broader applicability.
No code release or statement of availability is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the reported numbers given the sensitivity to λ, α, and configuration choices.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically relevant gap: how the choice of Kronecker component dimensions (r1, r2) and number of components r affects the capacity and performance of Kronecker adapters, which prior work (KronA, MoKA) treats as heuristic design choices.

The theoretical analysis is well-motivated: it extends the subspace-alignment framework of LoRA-One (Zhang et al., 2025) to the Kronecker setting using Kronecker-product SVD, and yields qualitative principles (small r1, large r2, r near or above r* but not excessive) that are then empirically validated in controlled ablations (Tables 3-8) and reproduced across backbones and modalities (Tables 18-24).

The proposed stabilization scaling factor (Theorem 3.4, lambda ~ 1/sqrt(r*r2)) is a simple, well-justified fix for gradient-norm sensitivity across configurations, with supporting gradient-norm plots (Figure 1) and an ablation (Table 17) that disentangles the contribution of component design from the scaling factor.

Experiments are broad: GLUE with T5-Base, GSM8k/HumanEval with LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen models, and seven image classification datasets with CLIP-ViT-B/16. CDKA achieves strong results (e.g., +1.31 points over LoRA-One on GSM8k, +5.14 over KronA on image classification) at a very low parameter count (0.41M on T5), and computational cost is comparable to LoRA (Table 15).

The paper is generally well written, with a clear problem decomposition (Section 3), honest identification of the rank-vs-performance inconsistency (Table 2), and a limitations section acknowledging the linear-only theoretical scope.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely an adaptation of existing linear alignment analysis (proofs explicitly adapted from Zhang et al., 2025 and Stoeger & Soltanolkotabi, 2021). The analysis is restricted to linear models, gradient descent (while experiments use AdamW), Gaussian isotropic inputs, and regime conditions (r* <= r < 2r*, etc.). The bridge from these asymptotic alignment results to the concrete heuristics (r* in [2,8]) is only empirical, so the theory-practice connection is looser than the framing suggests.

The closest related methods, MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025) and MoKA-MoE (Yu et al., 2025), are excluded from all head-to-head comparisons due to 'substantial computational overhead'. Since MoKA directly addresses heterogeneous component dimensions and CDKA claims to subsume/improve KronA-style adapters, the absence of this comparison weakens the SOTA claims.

On NLU (Table 9), CDKA (87.30 average) is clearly below LoRA-One (88.73) and GoRA (87.96), and below full fine-tuning by 0.61; the 'near-optimal using only 12.5% of trainable parameters' claim is defensible but the paper's headline framing overstates overall dominance. On HumanEval, CDKA (24.59) is also slightly behind LoRA-GA/GoRA.

Several ablations and validation experiments (Tables 3-8, Figure 1) are conducted on a single task (GSM8k with LLaMA-2-7B) and a single configuration; while appendix Tables 18-24 partially mitigate this, the core evidence base for the three principles is narrow relative to the generality of the claims.

The practical guidelines are partly heuristic: e.g., r* is found empirically to lie in [2,8], and r1 in [2,4] is recommended 'empirically'; the connection to the theoretical bound on alpha (Eq. 12) is not directly verified in practice.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract is truncated ('Code is available a'), and the mapping between the theoretical orderings (which only constrain alignment, not final loss) and the derived 'principles' involves unstated inferential steps.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored question: how the component configuration (r1, r2, r) of Kronecker adapters governs their capacity, which prior works (KronA, MoKA, MoKA-MoE) treat as heuristic choices.

The theoretical analysis connects component design to subspace alignment with the first-step gradient of full fine-tuning (Theorems 3.2, B.1, C.1), yielding concrete, testable principles (small r1, large r2, moderate r).

The derived guidelines are validated not only on the development setting (LLaMA-2-7B/GSM8k, Tables 3-8) but also on additional backbones and modalities (Tables 18-24), which strengthens the empirical case.

Experiments span NLU (GLUE), NLG (GSM8k, HumanEval), and CV (seven CLIP classification datasets) with multiple models (T5, LLaMA-2-7B/3.1-8B/3-70B, Qwen-3, CLIP), and Table 17 cleanly disentangles the contribution of component design from the stabilization scaling factor.
Computational costs are measured (Table 15) and the Kronecker reformulation (Eq. 17) shows the method introduces no inference or training overhead relative to LoRA at matched parameters.
The limitations section honestly notes the restriction of the theory to linear settings.
weaknesses: The theoretical machinery is largely adapted from prior work: Lemma B.2 is explicitly 'adapted from Lemma C.5 in Zhang et al. (2025)' and Lemma B.4 from the same paper; the core alignment framework, sub-Gaussian data model, and one-step gradient analysis are inherited from LoRA-One. The genuinely new technical content is a specialization of this framework to the Kronecker structure, which is incremental.

There is a substantial gap between what the theory proves and what the method recommends. The alignment analysis concerns gradient descent on a linear model with isotropic Gaussian inputs at initialization, yet the guidelines actually deployed (r1 ∈ [2,4], r* ∈ [2,8]) are justified mostly by GSM8k ablations. Notably, the theory predicts alignment improves with larger r (probability terms decay as exp(-r)), while the paper's third 'principle' says increasing r does not help — this principle appears empirical rather than derived, weakening the claim that guidelines follow from the analysis.

Headline empirical claims are overstated relative to the strongest baselines. On GLUE, CDKA (87.30 average) clearly underperforms LoRA-One (88.73) and LoRA-GA (87.77); on HumanEval it is second to GoRA. 'State-of-the-art' and 'near-optimal' characterizations rely mainly on GSM8k and CLIP results.

The most closely related method, MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025), is excluded from all experiments on compute grounds, so the paper's central claim — that principled component design supersedes manual/mixture-based design — is never tested head-to-head against the alternative that motivates it. MoKA-MoE is likewise absent.

The motivating 'inconsistency' analysis (Table 2) uses only GSM8k with two configurations; given that the entire paper rests on the observation that rank alone does not determine performance, this evidence base is thin, and comparable motivation across tasks/models is missing.

The stabilization analysis (Theorem 3.4) is heuristic: it relies on a first-order expansion (O(λ²) approximations) and a variance-scale argument to conclude λ = Θ(1/√(r·r2)), and the constant α remains a tuned hyperparameter (16-64 across models, Table 16), so the 'principled' scaling reduces to another tuned quantity in practice.

Some robustness tables (21-24) lack standard deviations entirely, and several comparisons in the main tables involve the authors' own reimplementations with hyperparameters 'aligned' to original papers, which is difficult to verify.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Code is available a'), Table 1 contains an apparent typo in the full fine-tuning row (r1, r2 = 1, d_in or r1, r2 = d_out, 1), and initialization ablations (Table 8) cover only a single configuration.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored question: how the component configuration (r1, r2, r) of Kronecker adapters governs their capacity. The motivating observation in Table 2 (that rank alone is a necessary but insufficient indicator of performance) is a clear, well-supported empirical finding.

The theoretical analysis via Kronecker product SVD extends the subspace-alignment framework of LoRA-One (Zhang et al., 2025) to the Kronecker setting, yielding concrete, testable design principles (small r1, large r2, moderate r). The proofs in Appendix B-C are substantial and the derivation structure (linearization, error bound, alignment) is coherent.

The stabilization scaling factor (Theorem 3.4, lambda = alpha/sqrt(r*r2)) is a practical contribution, and Figure 1 convincingly demonstrates that gradient norms become invariant to component configuration.

The experimental evaluation is broad: NLU (GLUE/T5-Base), mathematical reasoning (LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, LLaMA-3-70B, Qwen-3-0.6B/8B), code generation, and image classification (CLIP-ViT-B/16), with three random seeds, ablation studies (Tables 17-24), a 'default configuration' robustness check (Table 14), and computational cost comparison (Table 15).
Limitations are honestly discussed (linear-setting analysis only), hyperparameters and implementation details are provided, and code availability is promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The closest related method, MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025), is excluded from all main experiments on the grounds of computational overhead, and MoKA-MoE likewise. Since MoKA is precisely the sum-of-Kronecker-components formulation with heterogeneous component dimensions that this paper analyzes, the absence of a direct comparison is a significant evidential gap: the claim that principled component design 'substantially improves the performance of Kronecker adapters' is only demonstrated against KronA, a much weaker baseline.

The theoretical results are largely an adaptation of the LoRA-One analysis; the design principles (Remark 3.3) are read off from the direction of dependence of looser-vs-tighter bounds (Eq. 12-13), which is a fairly indirect argument. The alignment analysis assumes isotropic Gaussian inputs and a linear loss, and the paper provides no empirical verification that the measured subspace alignment actually tracks the predicted r1/r2/r dependence in practice.

Theorem 3.4's 'if and only if' claim is loose: the scaling analysis (Eqs. 42-46) is a first-order (early-training) argument with O(lambda^2) remainder terms, and the claimed Theta(r2) variance scale of Kaiming initialization glosses over r1-dependence, yet the resulting lambda depends on r and r2 but not r1.

The empirical gains over the strongest baselines are modest in places: +1.31 points over LoRA-One on GSM8k (LLaMA-2-7B), second-best on HumanEval (behind GoRA), and +0.51 average on CLIP where the LoRA-One numbers are the authors' own reimplementation. Additionally, the NLU configuration (r1=r2=3, r=1) is chosen somewhat ad hoc and sits uneasily with the stated principle of preferring r1 << r2, weakening the sharpness of the guidelines.

The component-design ablations (Tables 3-8) are validated primarily on a single task (GSM8k with LLaMA-2-7B), although Appendix F partially compensates with Qwen and CLIP results; standard deviations in some ablation tables are small enough that the trends for r1 (Table 3, where the best and worst values differ by ~1 point) are not clearly statistically meaningful.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Code is available a'), and there are notation inconsistencies in the appendix (e.g., 'Bft' defined with vec(A) entries in the Part 1 setup of the proof; mixed use of G^f_0 and Ge0 in Theorem B.3), which should be corrected.
